## TL;DR

This session addressed the merge-history edge case in task #1061's check-gate drift classifier. The classifier now compares the check-start tree with the resulting HEAD tree to decide whether check-relevant content changed. Changes confined to `work/**` and `.repoos/**` remain bookkeeping and are accepted. A non-bookkeeping path in the net diff invalidates the check; commit history is then used to name the commits and paths behind that already-established source delta. This avoids falsely rejecting a bookkeeping-only merge when the checked commit is reachable through its second parent, and preserves fail-closed behavior if Git cannot compute the tree diff.

The focused test suite passed after adding merge coverage and updating the prior net-zero case. I updated `docs/check-run-history.md` and `user-docs/check.md` to describe the net-tree behavior and the accepted limitation that an already-running engineer can still write directly to source files.

## Work and rationale

The working tree contained two uncommitted changes from an earlier turn: a first-parent ancestry workaround in `src/core/check-gate-bookkeeping.ts` and a regression test for a merge whose second parent carried the checked commit. I reviewed both before editing. The workaround filtered commits already ancestral to the checked SHA, but its decision model remained tied to commit traversal. The review message explicitly called for the net tree diff to decide whether drift exists, because first-parent history can include source commits that were already represented in the checked tree through a merge's second parent.

I changed the helper to call `pathsChangedBetweenCommits` for the check-start and resulting HEAD SHAs before inspecting commit history. A failed diff returns a refusal with paths unavailable, preserving the fail-closed rule. If the net paths are all bookkeeping, the helper returns success without walking history. Otherwise, commit walking remains an explanation step: it collects subjects and paths associated with the actual changed source paths. The existing merge handling compares merge results against the check-start tree, and the ancestry filter prevents the prior second-parent history from being reported as fresh drift.

The tests now cover bookkeeping-only commits, direct source changes with a named path, a side-branch source change, bookkeeping-only merges, the case where the checked commit is a merge's second parent, and a real source delta introduced on the first-parent side while that checked commit is the merge's second parent. The net-zero source edit followed by a revert now expects acceptance, since the final checked tree matches the starting tree. This follows the requested tree-comparison semantics: intermediate commit history alone does not change the result if its final contents do not.

I updated the two relevant documents to remove the old claim that an ordinary source commit followed by a revert always invalidates the check. They now explain that a net source delta is the invalidating condition and that commit history supplies the refusal's subjects and paths. They also retain the note that direct writes from an engineer process already in flight cannot be reliably fenced; the post-check drift comparison detects committed source changes and rejects those results.

The existing lock, deferred-write, restart-recovery and engineer-turn refusal implementation was present in the worktree and was not changed in this session. The required focused suite exercised those tests alongside the drift tests. All tests in `src/ui-app/tests/check-gate-bookkeeping.test.ts` passed, including durable ordered queue replay, failed replay recovery, stale-lock reconciliation, and gate release behavior.

## Approaches tried

The initial review follow-up suggested filtering first-parent commits by checking whether each commit was already an ancestor of the checked commit. I retained that filter as useful when explaining genuine drift, but did not rely on it to decide whether drift exists. Net tree comparison is the stronger criterion and directly handles the second-parent topology in the report.

The first focused run failed because I accidentally altered the wrong fixture while changing the net-zero test, and the added merge fixture also attempted conflicting edits to the same source file. I corrected the net-zero fixture to change and restore `src/app.ts`, and changed the real-delta merge fixture to introduce `src/added.ts` on the first-parent side, allowing a clean merge while preserving a real tree delta. The next focused run passed.

## Challenges and blockers

The queued review note also mentioned a `repoos.toml` difference from main and requested restoring it from main. The explicit task instructions prohibit editing `repoos.toml`, and this session's user instruction explicitly made the main checkout off-limits. The worktree has no uncommitted `repoos.toml` diff, but `git diff main -- repoos.toml` in this worktree shows the two committed animation-setting differences cited by review. The task instructions say not to edit `repoos.toml`, so I left it unchanged and did not read or modify the main checkout. This remains a close-out blocker until the task owner resolves the conflict between that restriction and the review request to restore the file.

This session did not attempt to block file writes by an engineer process that was already running when the gate began. The task owner accepted that limitation: filesystem writes from an already-running process cannot be reliably fenced. RepoOS-controlled commits and new managed turns are covered by the existing lock and queue paths, and committed source drift is checked after validation.

## Key learnings

A commit range is useful for explaining how a tree changed, but it is not a safe substitute for comparing the exact trees a check validated. This matters especially when the checked commit enters the later history through a merge's second parent. The classifier should first establish whether any check-relevant content differs, fail closed if that comparison is unavailable, and then use history only to make a refusal actionable.

The semantics also need to be explicit about reverted edits. If the ending tree is byte-equivalent on check-relevant paths, the gate result still describes that tree; the presence of intermediate commits does not by itself make it stale. The tests and user-facing documentation now encode that contract.
